output:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, of Le Locle, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Girard, you are an établisseur from Le Locle. Tell me in your own words about this evening.

GIRARD: About the evening? I dined at the Monniers' as I have dined there for years, and I quarrelled with the master over the price of his repeater. I buy movements and parts from the Locle houses, I have them finished and cased, and I sell the watches under my firm's name. That is my trade. Monnier had a repeater on his bench that I wanted the rights to, so that I could have it made in quantity. He would not take my price. He said my price insulted the work, and I said the work was four years of his life and nobody was going to pay him for the years. We were both loud about it. Then the rest of them began talking about the New Year, and I let it go.

MATTHEY: Was there anything else said at dinner?

GIRARD: He asked to see my watch, as he asks everyone every year, and I would not show it to him. I am a merchant. I do not hand my watch to a man who will tell me what is wrong with it in front of his wife. I also told young Félix that I wanted what he owes me, and I told the doctor nothing, because I do not care for Dr Vauthier's company. He is a pleasant man and he knows it. He quotes Latin at a table where nobody asked him to.

MATTHEY: Go on, if you please.

GIRARD: After dinner I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. I heard the temple strike ten there. I did not look at my watch. A man who has been quarrelling does not look at his watch, he looks at the fire. Then I wanted air. I put on my coat and went out into the street to smoke. It was a hard cold, with old snow still in the gutters, and I walk in the cold when I want to think. I went out at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, and I stayed under the front windows of the house.

MATTHEY: You smoked there.

GIRARD: I smoke Brissago. They are cheap and they go out when you are not looking, but I cannot afford better at what I am paid. The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar, at twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. I heard it begin. I know nothing of the music. I am not a musician, Monsieur, I am a man who sells watches.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else from the house?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above. I was still under the front windows. I am not going to say more than I heard. Faint and quick, that is all I can give you, and I would not swear to more.

MATTHEY: You kept your watch in your hand.

GIRARD: A merchant notices time, Monsieur. It is my living. I looked at it when I went out, I looked at it when I heard the bells, and I looked at it when I came back.

MATTHEY: And when did you come back?

GIRARD: I came back into the house at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven, and its face showed two minutes past eleven. I did not think about it. I went straight up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Monsieur Girard. Is there anything you wish to add that I have not asked?

GIRARD: Only that I am sorry for the old man. We quarrelled, and he was a stubborn fool about his work, but I respected the work. There are not many left in the Jura who would spend four years on one movement without a thought for the price. Write that down, if you like. I want it on your paper.
